ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Sports Medicine Consultation — Rocky Marciano — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Two-week review on the day of the sports medicine consultation: back and leg pain, the thumb, home blood pressure, the brain health baseline and an exercise plan

text.paragraph: A 32-year-old retired professional heavyweight boxer, four months out of training, with a left L4-L5 disc herniation and L5 radiculopathy a few weeks old on a background of years of low back pain, post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the left thumb base, weight gain after stopping training, and a career of repetitive head impacts. Please advise on the back and leg, the thumb, a brain health baseline and an exercise plan for retirement. [S]

list.item: Does the disc herniation need repeat imaging or a surgical opinion now, and what would change that?
What exercise therapy do you advise for the radiculopathy and the chronic back pain, and when can he run and train again?
How should the post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the left thumb base be treated, and is an injection needed?
What should a brain health baseline after his career include, is brain imaging indicated, and how often should it be repeated?
What exercise and weight plan do you advise now that heavy training has stopped, and what should he avoid?

text.paragraph: Mr. Marciano, 32, a retired professional heavyweight boxer, is seen at the request of Dr. Fairweather-Obi two weeks after intake. Years of mechanical low back pain; a few weeks ago a left L4-L5 disc extrusion with L5 radiculopathy after bending to lift. The leg pain now comes only after sitting for an hour, and the foot numbness is fading; no weakness, saddle numbness or bladder or bowel change. Left thumb base pain on pinch and grip, after an old fracture from his early fighting years. About thirteen years of Army, amateur and professional boxing with heavy sparring; he recalls no loss of consciousness and has no headache, memory, mood, behavior, sleep or balance complaints. He stopped training four months ago and has gained about 9 kg. Naproxen once or twice a day with food and diclofenac gel on the thumb. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Rocco Francis Marchegiano was born on September 1, 1923, in Brockton, Massachusetts, where his father, Pierino, worked in a shoe factory; he later boxed as Rocky Marciano. [D]
As a small child he had pneumonia and was not expected to survive. [D]
He was drafted into the Army in 1943, served in Britain, and completed his service in March 1946 at Fort Lewis, Washington; he took up boxing in the Army. [D]
He turned professional in March 1947 and won the world heavyweight championship on September 23, 1952, in Philadelphia, knocking out Jersey Joe Walcott in the thirteenth round. [D]
Broken hands, back injuries and many facial cuts were among the injuries he had during his career. [D]

By one account he knew from August 1949 that he was fighting with a ruptured disc in his back, and from 1951 he had an arthritic right elbow that left his right arm slightly shorter than the left. [D]
He was unbeaten as a professional, retiring with 49 wins in 49 bouts, 43 by knockout; he is the only heavyweight champion to retire with a perfect record. [D]
He trained exceptionally hard: more than once he sparred about 250 rounds to prepare for a fight, about 100 more than usual, and he limited his diet. [D]

On April 27, 1956, at 32, he announced his retirement as undefeated heavyweight champion, saying he wanted to spend more time with his family. Accounts also mention that he was weary of training, at odds with his manager over money, did not want to fight past his prime, and had an ailing back. [D]
In July 1956, after he felt pain in his back while playing with his three-year-old daughter, he checked into a hospital and was diagnosed with a ruptured disc in his back. [D]
He married in 1950; he and his wife had a daughter and later adopted a son. [D]

list.item: Disc herniation: imaging and surgery (M51.16). An improving left L5 radiculopathy with no motor deficit and no red flags. Most such herniations improve within six to twelve weeks without surgery, and repeat imaging would not change the plan. A surgical opinion would be needed for any new weakness, saddle numbness or bladder or bowel change (the same day), or for disabling leg pain that has not improved after six to twelve weeks of good conservative care. [S]

Exercise therapy and return to training (M54.59). Exercise therapy is the main treatment for both the radiculopathy and the chronic back pain: directional preference (extension) exercise, which centralizes his pain today, then motor control and progressive trunk and hip strengthening, twice a week for six weeks, then a home program. Naproxen with food is reasonable for a short course but should be needed less as therapy works; if he needs it most days he should say so rather than keep taking it. No opioids or muscle relaxants. Walking and swimming now; slow jogging on the flat once the leg pain has been gone for a few weeks; no heavy lifting from the floor for three months. [S]

Thumb-base osteoarthritis (M18.32). Post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the left first carpometacarpal joint. A hand-based thumb orthosis has the strongest support and was fitted today, to wear for gripping work and at night, with hand therapy exercises and continued topical diclofenac. A corticosteroid injection is an option if pain persists after six to twelve weeks of this; it is not needed now. [S]

Brain health baseline (Z87.828). A normal baseline: no cognitive, mood, behavioral, sleep or balance complaints, a normal neurological screen, MoCA 29, PHQ-9 3, GAD-7 4 and a PROMIS sleep T-score of 55 with back pain at night. Traumatic encephalopathy syndrome is a research diagnosis under the 1951 NINDS consensus criteria, which require progressive core clinical features; he has none, and the diagnosis is not made on a history of exposure alone. Brain imaging is not indicated without new symptoms or signs. The baseline should be repeated yearly, with earlier review for any change in memory, mood, behavior, speech or movement; he should avoid sparring and other head impacts. [S]

Exercise and weight after heavy training (E66.3). His energy needs have fallen sharply while his eating has not. A target of 5% to 7% weight loss over six months is realistic: 150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity and strength training twice a week, smaller portions with less salt, and a week of home blood pressure readings before each review. His current home average of 126/78 mmHg is in the elevated range and should improve with this. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Fairweather-Obi's intake note and today's two-week note. Outside lumbar MRI report: left paracentral L4-L5 disc extrusion contacting the left L5 root, no stenosis elsewhere. Hand X-ray: first carpometacarpal narrowing with a small osteophyte and a healed old fracture at the base of the first metacarpal. Intake laboratory tests: creatinine 1.08 mg/dL, hemoglobin 15.2 g/dL, HbA1c 5.4%, LDL 137 mg/dL. MoCA 29, PHQ-9 3, GAD-7 4, PROMIS sleep T-score 55, Oswestry 36%. Today: back pain 5 out of 10, thumb pain 5 out of 10, grip 38 kg left and 54 kg right, FIHOA 9 out of 30; home blood pressure average 126/78 mmHg. [S]

list.item: No repeat imaging and no surgical opinion now; a surgical opinion for any new weakness, saddle numbness or bladder or bowel change, or for disabling leg pain beyond six to twelve weeks. [S]
Physical therapy twice a week for six weeks (extension-based exercise, motor control and strengthening), then a home program. [S]
Naproxen with food only as long as needed, and tell Dr. Fairweather-Obi if he needs it most days; no opioids or muscle relaxants. [S]
Walking and swimming now; slow jogging once the leg pain has been gone for a few weeks; no heavy lifting from the floor for three months. [S]
Thumb orthosis (fitted today) for gripping work and at night, hand exercises and topical diclofenac; an injection only if pain persists after six to twelve weeks. [S]
Brain health baseline repeated yearly; no brain imaging without new symptoms or signs; no sparring or other head impacts. [S]
150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity, strength training twice a week, and a 5% to 7% weight loss goal over six months. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Fairweather-Obi, who saw him the same day. Mr. Marciano asked whether boxing had harmed his brain; he was told that his baseline today is normal, that no test can predict the future for one person, and that keeping fit, sleeping well and avoiding further head impacts are the steps that help. He asked when he could run again and was given the graded plan. [S]
Follow-up: Sports medicine review on request if the leg pain has not settled by twelve weeks or the thumb has not improved; Dr. Fairweather-Obi continues his care at eight and twelve weeks. [S]
